narrative: I am submitting this complaint against Wells Fargo regarding its denial of my fraud claim involving 18 unauthorized debit-card transactions totaling $5600.00. The transactions occurred between approximately and , and appeared under merchant descriptions including and . I did not initiate, authorize, approve, participate in, or receive any benefit from any of these transactions. Before discovering the fraud, I was experiencing serious medical circumstances that substantially impaired my ability to regularly monitor and reconcile my account activity. Any delay in discovering the charges was caused solely by those medical circumstances. It was not intentional and did not constitute authorization, approval, ratification, or acceptance of the transactions. Regulation E requires a financial institution to reasonably extend the applicable notification periods when a delay resulted from extenuating circumstances. The official interpretation identifies hospitalization as an example of circumstances requiring an extension. Notice is effective when a consumer takes steps reasonably necessary to provide the bank with pertinent information, and notice may be given by telephone. Wells Fargos stated reasons for denial Wells Fargo opened claim and denied it on . The online claim system provided only the generic statement : After careful review, your claim has been declined. Wells Fargo representatives subsequently advised me that the denial was based on : 1. The alleged timing of my report ; and 2. The fact that Wells Fargos records allegedly showed that I had logged into online banking during the period when the unauthorized transactions occurred. Wells Fargo also advised me that my complaint and disputed claim were being escalated to its Executive Offices. Neither alleged reason establishes that I authorized the transactions. Merely logging into online banking does not establish that I initiated a disputed purchase, authorized a merchant to debit my account, reviewed the particular transactions, understood that fraudulent activity had occurred, or received any benefit from the charges. Regulation E defines an unauthorized electronic fund transfer according to whether the transfer was initiated by someone other than the consumer, without actual authority, and without the consumer receiving a benefit. The CFPB also confirms that transfers made by a fraudster using stolen or fraudulently obtained account credentials remain unauthorized electronic fund transfers. A login event may be information Wells Fargo considers, but it is not conclusive proof of authorization or knowledge. The bank must identify the date and time of each login, the device and IP address involved, what pages or transaction information were actually displayed, whether the disputed charges were viewed, and whether the login session initiated or authenticated any particular disputed transaction. A general login record does not establish actual authority to initiate 18 separate merchant transactions. Regulation Es official interpretation further provides that even receipt of a periodic statement showing unauthorized transfers may be considered as one factor, but can not be treated as conclusive evidence that the consumer knew of the loss or theft of an access device. Therefore, an online-banking loginwithout proof of what was actually viewed or initiatedshould not automatically be treated as conclusive proof of knowledge or authorization. Under 15 U.S.C. 1693g, Wells Fargo bears the burden of proving either that the transfers were authorized or, if unauthorized, that all conditions permitting Wells Fargo to impose liability on me were satisfied. Except as permitted by that statute, a consumer incurs no liability for an unauthorized electronic fund transfer. The timing determination appears legally deficient Wells Fargo has not identified the date on which it transmitted each periodic statement first reflecting the disputed transactions. Regulation E generally measures the error-notification period from the date the financial institution sends the periodic statement containing the alleged errornot simply from the date the transaction occurred. Private card-network deadlines can not replace Regulation Es more protective statement-based notice period. Even when a bank asserts that notice was late, it can not automatically make the consumer responsible for every disputed transaction. For transactions occurring after the applicable 60-day period, Wells Fargo must establish that the later transfers would not have occurred had earlier notice been provided. It must also apply the mandatory reasonable extension for medical or other extenuating circumstances before imposing liability. Consumer negligence can not be used to impose liability greater than Regulation E permits. Accordingly, even if Wells Fargo believes I should have monitored my account differently, that belief does not establish authorization or eliminate the statutory liability protections. Temporary or provisional credit The Electronic Fund Transfer Act, 15 U.S.C. 1693f, and its implementing regulation, 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( c ), establish the applicable provisional-credit requirements. Wells Fargo was required to promptly investigate and ordinarily determine whether an error occurred within 10 business days after receiving my notice. If it could not complete a compliant investigation within 10 business days and elected to use the extended investigation period, it was required to provisionally credit my account for the amount of the alleged error within 10 business days, including applicable interest, and give me full use of those funds during the investigation. The ordinary extended investigation period is 45 days and may be as long as 90 days for qualifying point-of-sale debit-card transactions. The primary exceptions are when the bank timely required written confirmation of an oral claim but did not receive that written confirmation within 10 business days, or when the disputed account is a securities account governed by Regulation T. Wells Fargo has not informed me that either exception applies. Because Wells Fargo initially denied the claim within approximately two days, the provisional-credit obligation would not arise merely from the passage of those two days. However, if Wells Fargos Executive Offices have reopened or continued the investigation beyond the applicable 10-business-day period, Wells Fargo must provide provisional credit unless it can establish a lawful regulatory exception. Wells Fargo should not characterize the matter as an active or continuing Executive Office investigation while withholding the provisional credit required for an extended investigation. If the denial was merely an immediate preliminary determination and the Executive Offices are now conducting the actual investigation, I request that Wells Fargo provisionally credit the disputed $5600.00 while that investigation remains pending. Inadequate investigation and explanation An unauthorized electronic fund transfer is an error under Regulation E. Wells Fargo was required to conduct a prompt and reasonable investigation, review relevant information in its own records, and consider my assertion that the transactions were unauthorized. The CFPB has specifically found that a financial institution does not conduct a reasonable investigation when it summarily denies a dispute without considering relevant information, including the consumers assertion that the transfer was unauthorized. Regulation E does not permit a bank to limit its investigation to payment instructions when other information in its own records could help resolve the claim. Relevant information may include transaction history, transaction location, the payees location, records maintained by service providers, and any other information appropriate to resolve the dispute. When Wells Fargo determined that no error occurred, it was required to provide a written explanation of its findings, advise me of my right to request the documents relied upon, and promptly provide those documents upon request in an understandable form. The generic statement that my claim was declined did not satisfy my request for the specific factual basis of the denial. call with On , at approximately Pacific Time, I contacted Wells Fargo to request clarification and escalation. Throughout that time, I have taken my account security seriously, have never knowingly shared my online banking credentials, and have never authorized another individual to access my accounts. The transfer itself was highly unusual and inconsistent with my normal banking activity. This transaction was completely outside of my normal account usage, which I believe should have been considered as part of Wells Fargo 's investigation. Wells Fargo denied my claim and stated that it concluded I had authorized the transactions. However, I have never been provided with the evidence supporting that conclusion. In Wells Fargo 's response, the bank stated : " The transactions were online transactions and they were initially declined. The customer would have been notified by the merchant that the transactions were initially declined. The declined transactions were verified through our system and then were resubmitted by the merchant where they were then approved. '' This explanation raises several questions that have never been answered. The activity reflected on my account began with an electronic transfer from my savings account to my checking account, followed by withdrawals. It is unclear to me how the explanation regarding online merchant transactions and an verification relates to the transfer from my savings account. If Wells Fargo relied on an verification or other authentication to conclude that I authorized these transactions, I respectfully request that the bank explain exactly how that determination was made. I did not call Wells Fargo 's system to verify these transactions. I did not approve any fraud alert or verification request, nor did I authorize anyone else to do so. Likewise, I did not log into my Wells Fargo mobile application or online banking to initiate or authorize the transfer. If Wells Fargo 's investigation concluded that I did, I respectfully request that the bank provide the records supporting that conclusion. Specifically, I request that Wells Fargo provide : The exact date and timestamp of any login associated with the disputed transactions. Whether the login occurred through the Wells Fargo mobile application, online banking website, telephone banking, or another access channel. The IP address associated with the login. The device information or device identifier used. The authentication method used, including whether a password, biometric authentication, one-time passcode, or another method was used. Any records demonstrating that I personally initiated or authorized the transfer. The exact date and timestamp of any verification. The telephone number used during the interaction. The authentication method used during the verification. Any logs, recordings, or documentation associated with that verification. Any internal investigation notes or documentation explaining how Wells Fargo concluded that I authorized these transactions. To date, Wells Fargo has only stated its conclusion that I authorized the transactions. It has not explained the factual basis for that conclusion or provided the evidence it relied upon. Additionally, Wells Fargo previously referenced that my debit card remained in my possession during the disputed activity. However, the transactions I am disputing began with an electronic transfer from my savings account to my checking account. Possession of my physical debit card, by itself, does not establish that I personally authorized an electronic transfer or accessed my online banking. I respectfully believe Wells Fargo 's investigation was incomplete because it reached the conclusion that I authorized these transactions without providing the evidence supporting that determination. Given the unusual nature of the transfer, my immediate reporting of the unauthorized activity, and my long-standing banking relationship with Wells Fargo respectfully request that the investigation be reopened and that the bank produce the records supporting its decision. I am requesting the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau 's assistance in obtaining a complete explanation of Wells Fargo 's investigation, the evidence relied upon in denying my claim, and a fair reconsideration of my unauthorized electronic fund transfer dispute. My goal is to understand the factual basis for Wells Fargo 's determination and to ensure that my claim is evaluated based on objective evidence demonstrating that I personally authorized these transactions. If such evidence exists, I respectfully request that it be provided. If it does not, I ask that Wells Fargo reconsider its decision and provide appropriate relief.

narrative: I, , owner of , submit this complaint against Wells Fargo Bank N.A for its wrongful handling of a chargeback dispute ( reason code 10.4 - other fraud, card absent environment ) The financial harm to my business resulted from two distinct failures ; Wells Fargo 's failure to follow mandated dispute investigation procedures for card-not-present fraud and automatic deduction of transaction processing fees and dispute fees, which I was charged despite the dispute being incorrectly decided against me. Wells Fargo 's mishandling of this dispute led to an incorrect chargeback decision that caused direct and material financial harm to my business. MERCHANT ROLE IN THE TRANSACTION is a registered merchant operating on the platform, which uses as its payment processor. The following describes how transactions are processes in the environment, and why the merchant bears no responsibility for cardholder registration, verification or authorization. ( merchant ) has no involvement in bidder registration and does not handle, enter, or store any card credentials. The merchant does not perform and is not authorized to perform any verification, authentication, or authorization of payments. All cardholder data is transmitted directly and exclusively from the cardholder to . The merchant is never is possession of this information. Charges are processed and authorized automatically through 's secure, tokenized payment system entirely without merchant involvement. The merchant 's only visibility into a customer 's account is the name, billing and shipping addresses and last four digits of the card number - information already verified and authenticated by and the issuing bank prior to authorization. FACTS OF THE TRANSACTION On bidder registered on the platform. He purchased multiple lots of fine jewelry totaling $3800.00. Following the auction contacted via email and requested that the items be shipped to the shipping and billing address on file with the platform. A shipping and insurance fee of $120.00. fulfilled the order in the full compliance with platform procedures. The goods were delivered to the verified billing and shipping address provided by the buyer. The billing and shipping address were identical. On received notice of a chargeback dispute for the full amounts of $3800.00 and $120.00. All relevant evidence was promptly submitted to in response to the dispute. WELLS FARGO 'S DISPUTE DECISION ; On Wells Fargo issued its dispute decision in favor of the cardholder. The bank 's stated rationale was as follows : ( Our center has certified that this is an unauthorized transaction. The merchant provided no proof that our cardholder authorized the disputed transaction. Neither the name nor the address provided by the merchant matches our cardholder 's profile. The cardholder denies participation in the transaction, engagement with the merchant, or receipt of services. We have met all technical and certification requirements. The account was closed, placed on the exception file, and reported to as having been used fraudulently. Our cardholder is due full credit ) Wells Fargo categorized the dispute under Reason Code 10.4 ( other fraud card absent environment ) GROUNDS FOR COMPLAINT a ) The merchant can not provide authorization proof. Wells Fargo 's decision faults the merchant for failing to provide proof that the cardholder authorized the transaction. This requirement is factually and procedurally impossible to satisfy. As described above, has no role in the authorization process. The merchant never handles card credentials, does not interact with or Wells Fargo 's authorization system, and is not provided with any authorization codes, CVV results, or AVS response coded. The information merchant submitted- the buyer 's name, billing and shipping address is the information that presented to Wells Fargo during the authorization request. If that information did not match Wells Fargo 's records, the bank had both the ability and the obligation to decline the transaction at the point of authorization. WELLS FARGO FAILED ITS DUTY AT THE POINT OF AUTHORIZATION Under Rules and Product and Service Rules, when an authorization request is submitted, the issuing bank is responsible for verifying cardholder credentials including name, billing address, and card validation codes against its own records. If those credentials do not match the issuer is required to return a decline response, such as Response Code 93 ( transaction can not be completed ) By approving the tokenized request, Wells Fargo effectively certified that the credentials presented were valid and acceptable. The bank can not now claim that the name and address did not match its records, while simultaneously having approved the transaction. These positions are mutually contradictory. The merchant had no mechanism to perform these checks and no access to the results of any AVS or CVV verification. Chargeback liability can not be assigned to a party who is structurally excluded from the authorization process. ASSIGNEMENT OF CHARGEBACK LIABILITY VIOLATES CARD NETWORK RULES own rules prohibit issuers from assigning chargeback liability to merchant under the following circumstances ; Merchants did not process or authorize the transaction. Merchant relied on processor level ( ) authentication and tokenization. The issuer approved the transaction through its own authorization system. FINANCIAL HARM FROM INCORRECTLY ASSESSED FEES In addition to the chargeback amount itself, automatically deducted transaction processing fees and dispute fees from my account in connection with these chargebacks. These fees were assessed despite the fact that the dispute was incorrectly decided and the merchant bore no responsibility. RELIEF REQUESTED respectfully requests that the CFPB take the actions ; Direct Wells Fargo to reverse both chargebacks ( $3800.00 and $120.00 ), Direct Wells Fargo to reimburse all dispute fees assessed to as a result of this incorrectly decided dispute. I certify that the information in this complaint is true and accurate to the best of my knowledge. All supporting documentation will be submitted to this complaint. ( ) 2026

narrative: Subject : Failure to Explain Post-Complaint Cancellation of Force-Placed Insurance, Refund Calculation, and Related Account Adjustments I am submitting this complaint regarding Wells Fargo Bank , N.A.s handling of lender-placed hazard insurance imposed on my mortgage account and Wells Fargos subsequent failure to provide a complete explanation, supporting documentation, or accounting concerning the cancellation of that policy and the resulting refund. The identity of the individual, department, vendor, insurer, or third party that initiated, requested, approved, or authorized the cancellation. Whether the cancellation was related in any way to issues raised in CFPB Complaint No. . The dates used in calculating the refund. The period of coverage for which premiums were retained. The period of coverage for which premiums were refunded. Any calculation worksheets. Whether all account balances were properly adjusted. Whether prior escrow calculations were revised. Whether prior default-related calculations were revised. The omission of this information prevents meaningful evaluation of the circumstances surrounding the cancellation and refund. Accordingly, I request that Wells Fargo provide : 1. Documentation showing where the refund was applied. 12. This complaint does not challenge Wells Fargos ability to state that a cancellation occurred. Rather, it concerns Wells Fargos failure to explain why the cancellation occurred, how the refund was calculated, how the account was adjusted, and why the supporting records have not been provided despite repeated requests. narrative: I am submitting a formal complaint regarding a travel reservation booked through American Express Travel and the manner in which promotional benefits were presented to me during the booking process. During that process, American Express prominently advertised a package of benefits associated with my booking, including : A $600.00 hotel statement credit rewards points A $250.00 on-site hotel credit at the As a reasonable consumer, I relied on these advertised benefits when making my purchasing decision. As a consumer, I reasonably believed that promotions displayed to me within my authenticated American Express account were applicable to my account. I had no reason to believe otherwise. In fact, the purpose of logging into a customer account is to receive information and offers that are relevant to that specific customer relationship. My complaint is not based on a disagreement with the existence of terms and conditions. Rather, it is based on the fact that American Express presented these promotional benefits to a logged-in customer whose card type was already known to the company. A reasonable consumer should not be expected to assume that prominently displayed promotional benefits shown within a personalized booking experience do not apply to them. Nor should consumers be expected to search through extensive terms and conditions to determine whether American Express is displaying benefits for which they are ineligible despite knowing the card product associated with the account. The advertised benefits were material to my purchasing decision. Had I known that I would not receive the advertised $600.00 statement credit, the anticipated rewards earnings, and the $250.00 hotel property credit, I would have reevaluated my options and may have booked directly with the hotel or through another provider. These benefits represented a significant portion of the overall value proposition that influenced my decision to proceed with a prepaid reservation exceeding $5700.00. After discovering that I would not receive the advertised benefits, I made multiple good-faith attempts to resolve the issue directly with American Express On , I initiated an online chat with American Express. During that conversation, the representative informed me that the benefit was associated with what they described as " the '' and indicated that my was not eligible. The representative I spoke with was unable to assist and advised that I would need to speak with American Express . When I requested escalation to a manager, the call was disconnected. I called a third time and ultimately spoke with a supervisor named . During that conversation, acknowledged that he understood how a reasonable consumer could be confused by the manner in which the promotion was presented. He recognized that the advertising and booking experience could lead a cardmember to believe they were eligible for the advertised benefits. However, despite acknowledging the confusion, advised that the only resolution he could offer was cancellation of the reservation. He stated that he was unable to provide any goodwill accommodation, statement credit, points adjustment, travel credit, or any other remedy. American Express had the ability to identify my card type before displaying the promotion and before accepting my prepaid reservation. The burden should not be placed on consumers to discover exclusions hidden within terms and conditions when American Express already possesses the information necessary to determine eligibility and tailor promotional displays accordingly. I respectfully request that American Express review this matter and provide an appropriate resolution. At a minimum, I request consideration of a goodwill accommodation reasonably equivalent to the value of the benefits that were advertised and relied upon during the booking process. I further request that American Express review its marketing and booking practices to ensure that promotional offers are not displayed to logged-in cardmembers who are known to be ineligible for those benefits. After the freeze, I went to a Wells Fargo branch and provided a written explanation along with screenshots of the promotional offer and the check. A banker emailed this documentation directly to Wells Fargos fraud department. Wells Fargo subsequently reopened my account, which demonstrates that the original freeze and closure were not supported by valid evidence and should never have occurred. Despite this, on , Wells Fargo froze and closed my account again for the exact same reason, without any new information, communication, or investigation. When I called the fraud department, the first representative told me that these issues often get rereviewed and confirmed that this was the same issue as before. When I escalated the call, the next representative told me the decision was final and that there was no further escalation available. '' Reporting a bank-initiated closure as a consumer-initiated closure is a direct violation of FCRA accuracy standards. A furnisher 's investigation into a consumer dispute can not be a superficial automated check ; courts have consistently held that the FCRA requires a reasonable, substantive investigation of the underlying evidence. narrative: The issue concerns my Everyday Checking account with Wells Fargo Bank. Reasonable consumers would expect such material account changes to be clearly disclosed through direct email notifications, postal mail, and/or prominent placement on the first page of account statements well in advance of the effective date. Instead, the disclosure appeared to be buried in an obscure section of the statement where many customers would likely miss it. narrative: Summary : I am filing this complaint against Wells Fargo Bank , N.A . ( " Wells Fargo '' ) regarding a 30-day late payment that was reported on my credit file in . The late payment was caused by Wells Fargo 's mishandled conversion of my ( ending ) to a Wells Fargo Visa ( ending ). During the transition, Wells Fargo left me without any functional way to pay my outstanding balance, and without effective notice that my established payment channel had been disabled, while continuing to allow purchases on the original card up to the deactivation date. I am a customer with a deliberate, well-established system for paying every credit account on time, and I have an otherwise perfect payment history. This single derogatory mark is the direct result of Wells Fargo 's flawed process, not any failure or unwillingness on my part. I am asking the CFPB to assist in having Wells Fargo retract the 30-day late notation from all three major credit bureaus ( and ) My Established Payment Practices : This incident is not characteristic of how I manage my credit. I maintain a strict and deliberate payment discipline : I pay every credit card balance every month, and frequently every 20 days, well within the due date. I have all my other credit accounts set up with mobile notifications and routine payment habits. I have never had a late payment on any credit account prior to this incident. I had accumulated rewards points on my , demonstrating my active engagement with the account and my financial capacity to handle a $24.00 balance with no difficulty. I had both the intent and the means to pay this account on time. What I did not have was a functioning channel through which Wells Fargo would accept that payment during the transition period. What Happened, Timeline : I became aware of the following events and communications only after I noticed a drop in my credit score ; I did not connect these notifications to an active payment obligation at the time, in part because the app my established account interface, which I continued to log into, showed no balance owed and no in-app payment prompt. , emailed me that my Wells Fargo would be deactivated on and that any remaining balance would be transferred to a new Wells Fargo Visa . , emailed that my statement was ready, showing rewards points available, demonstrating active account engagement. , small purchases totaling $24.00 posted to the ( ending ) : $1.00, $16.00, and $7.00. These were the only charges on the account. , Wells Fargo internally converted the to a Wells Fargo Visa with a new account number ending . The app continued to show the original card but no longer offered any way to pay the balance. , Visa statement issued with a $24.00 new balance and a due date. No payment channel I had been using was available. , Second statement issued showing the $24.00 carried over as past-due plus a $1.00 minimum interest charge ( new balance : $25.00 ), with a notice that this is an attempt to collect a debt. , Wells Fargo emailed confirming the conversion had occurred on and instructing me to confirm and activate the new Visa Card before I could spend on it. , Third statement issued with another $1.00 minimum interest charge ( new balance : $26.00 ), again carrying the original charges as past-due. , The new Wells Fargo Visa was finally activated. I paid the entire outstanding balance of $26.00 in full immediately upon activation. The account is now current. , I installed the Wells Fargo mobile app for the first time. : Wells Fargo reported the account as 30 days past due to the credit bureaus, as reflected on the credit report dated . I paid the entire balance of $26.00 in full on , immediately upon activating the card. The account is now current. Why Wells Fargo 's Process Does Not Make Sense : The most basic expectation a consumer can have when a financial institution converts one credit card to another is that the existing account remains payable through its existing channel at least until the open statement is settled. Wells Fargo did not honor that expectation. Wells Fargo allowed continued purchases on the through the app, but disabled the ability to pay the balance through that same app. There is no logical or consumer-friendly reason for this asymmetry. From a consumer protection standpoint, allowing a customer to incur charges while disabling the means to pay them is the definition of a foreseeable, avoidable harm. The app remains active to this day and still does not offer a way to pay the Wells Fargo card. Wells Fargo did not push customers to the Wells Fargo app, did not send mobile or in-app notifications through any application I had installed, and relied on physical mail as the primary channel of notice for a digital-first payment account. Wells Fargo 's own conversion email confirms that, even after the conversion was complete, customers still had to confirm and activate the new card before they could use it. Combined with the unusable app, this created a multi-month window in which the account had a balance and incurred fees but had no functional payment channel. Why the Late-Payment Reporting Is Inaccurate and Unfair : The lateness was caused by Wells Fargo disabling my payment channel without providing a working alternative or effective notice. I had the funds, the rewards balance, and the established habit to pay this account on time. I was prevented from doing so by the conversion process itself. The moment a payment channel became available again on , I paid the balance in full. My otherwise perfect payment history demonstrates that this is not a pattern of behavior, it is a single, externally caused event. My credit report dated shows five additional credit accounts ( , , , , Bank ) every single one with a " Never late '' status. The Wells Fargo 30-day late mark is the only negative item across my entire credit history. Reporting this as a 30-day late payment misrepresents the actual circumstances and unfairly damages my credit profile, which I have worked hard to maintain. Prior Contact with Wells Fargo : I contacted Wells Fargo by phone to discuss this issue. The agent suggested the issue might " fix itself in the next cycle. '' However,, my credit report dated shows the account marked " 30 days past due as of '' with a " Potentially Negative '' designation, contradicting the agent 's representation. Wells Fargo 's frontline customer service was unable to address the credit reporting issue. The matter has not been resolved to my satisfaction, which is why I am now seeking the assistance of the CFPB.

narrative: What happened : This matter centers on Wells Fargos failure to evaluate the controlling evidence in a billing dispute : the transaction-dated sales documentation. On , jewelry containing blue diamonds was purchased from for approximately $25000.00 using a Wells Fargo credit account. The only reliable and verifiable record of what was disclosed at the time of sale is the transaction documentation provided at purchase, including the sales receipt, jewelry tags, and merchant appraisal. These documents do not contain any written disclosure that the blue diamonds were color-enhanced or treated. After the sale, an independent gemological report, obtained at my expense, confirmed that the diamonds are color-enhanced/ treated. This did not create the issue ; it revealed that a material characteristic affecting value existed but was not disclosed in the transaction documentation. On , a billing dispute was opened with Wells Fargo for goods not as described. Between and , Wells Fargo denied the dispute and multiple appeals. On , , and , three separate complaints were filed with the CFPB due to the companys failure to address the absence of written disclosure. Across all disputes and complaints, Wells Fargo did not identify any transaction-dated document showing that gemstone treatment was disclosed in writing at the time of sale. Instead of evaluating the actual sales documentation, Wells Fargo relied on merchant statements obtained after the transaction, interpretations of product descriptions, and appraisal-based arguments. These sources are not equivalent to the transaction record and do not establish what was disclosed at the time of purchase. This is the central failure. Regulatory standards exist specifically to prevent this type of situation and to ensure consumer protection through verifiable documentation. These include : - Regulation Z ( 12 CFR 1026.13 ), requiring a reasonable investigation based on the transaction record - The Fair Credit Billing Act, requiring evaluation of whether goods were accurately described based on what was provided at the time of sale - FTC Jewelry Guides ( 16 CFR Part 23 ), requiring disclosure of gemstone treatments that materially affect value clearly and conspicuously at the time of sale These standards require that disclosure be made in writing at the time of the transaction so that it can be verified. They do not rely on recollection, interpretation, or statements made after the fact. In this case : - The diamonds were confirmed to be treated by an independent report obtained after purchase - Treatment materially affects value - The transaction-dated sales documentation contains no written disclosure of treatment - Wells Fargo has not produced any document showing that such disclosure exists Wells Fargo also stated it could not determine what was discussed at the time of sale, yet still concluded the goods were properly described. When disclosure is required to be in writing, the transaction documentation is the controlling evidence. If the documentation does not contain the disclosure, then it was not disclosed. A reasonable investigation requires verification of disclosure within the transaction documentation. That did not occur. On , Wells Fargo issued a final response maintaining its denial without identifying any transaction-dated document showing disclosure of gemstone treatment. To date, across all internal disputes, appeals, and CFPB complaints, Wells Fargo has not produced any evidence demonstrating that the required disclosure occurred in the sales documentation. The central issue remains unresolved : - A material characteristic affecting value ( treatment ) exists - Required written disclosure is absent from the transaction documentation - The investigation did not evaluate or resolve that absence By relying on post-sale statements instead of the documented transaction record, the investigation did not address the controlling evidence. Given that the required disclosure must be verifiable in the transaction documentation and no such documentation has been identified, the determination appears unsupported by the record and raises concerns that the investigation did not meet the standards required under Regulation Z and the Fair Credit Billing Act for resolving billing disputes involving goods not as described.

narrative: We are filing a complaint regarding approximately $3000.00 in credit card interest charges accrued between and in our Wells Fargo checking account that we believe resulted from a materially misleading payment and disclosure system. The payment interface prominently emphasizes the minimum payment, while failing to clearly and conspicuously communicate that paying less than the full statement balance will immediately trigger high-interest charges ( often exceeding 20 % APR ). In practice, customers rely on the app interface, which highlights the minimum payment and due date, while the full statement balance is not presented with equal clarity. The key information required to avoid interest is therefore effectively obscured. Taken together, these design choices create a system where customers are steered toward incurring interest charges without clear, timely, and actionable disclosure. This is not an isolated incident, but a structural issue that benefits the bank financially while impairing the customers ability to make informed decisions. In our case, this resulted in approximately $3000.00 in interest charges accruing before we were able to identify the issue. We had sufficient funds to pay the full balance at all times. This was not a matter of inability or refusal to pay, but a direct result of a misleading and non-transparent user experience. Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E, once a consumer gives timely notice of an alleged error, the financial institution must investigate the alleged error, determine whether an error occurred, and report the results to the consumer within the required time. If the institution can not complete the investigation within 10 business days, it may use provisional credit, but the investigation still must be concluded within the applicable regulatory period, and the consumer must have full use of the provisionally credited funds during the investigation. 15 U.S.C. 1693f ( a ), ( c ). Wells Fargos response does not provide the factual basis necessary to justify denial. The letter says only that Wells Fargo did not identify evidence that the payment was made by an alternate method, could not locate charges on an alternate Wells Fargo account, and found the disputed transactions consistent with prior undisputed activity. Those are generalized conclusions, not a transaction-specific explanation showing what records were reviewed, what merchant or network data was obtained, what account evidence was compared, or how Wells Fargo determined that the disputed transactions were actually authorized by me. Regulation E requires a real investigation and a written explanation of findings if the bank concludes no error occurred. 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( c ), ( d ). The CFPBs official commentary also makes clear that a financial institution must begin its investigation promptly upon receipt of an oral notice and may not delay until it receives written confirmation. It also states that if an error occurred, the institution must correct the error, including refunding any fees imposed by the institution, where applicable. 12 C.F.R. Part 1005, Official Interpretations to 1005.11 ( c ). I also dispute Wells Fargos apparent effort to rely on prior undisputed activity, receipt of benefit, or a broad transaction pattern instead of proving authorization of the disputed transfers. Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E, consumer liability for unauthorized electronic fund transfers is limited by law, and the bank must comply with Regulation E before imposing liability on the consumer for an unauthorized EFT claim. 15 U.S.C. 1693g ( a ) ; 12 C.F.R. 1005.6 ( b ) ; Official Interpretations to 1005.11 ( b ). The response is also deficient because it does not provide the documentation underlying Wells Fargos determination. If a financial institution determines that no error occurred, it must provide an explanation of its findings, include notice of the consumers right to request the documents relied upon, and, upon request, promptly provide reproductions of the documents it relied on. 15 U.S.C. 1693f ( d ) ; 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( d ) ( 1 ). The CFPBs official commentary further states that the institution must provide copies in understandable form. I am therefore formally requesting that Wells Fargo produce all documents and data it relied upon in denying my claim and reversing the provisional credit, including but not limited to internal claim notes, transaction logs, account comparisons, merchant information, network records, screenshots, and any other material used to conclude that no error occurred. Regulation E expressly provides that those documents must be produced upon request. I also dispute Wells Fargos refusal to refund the overdraft fees listed in its own response. Wells Fargo identified overdraft fees of $35.00 each, totaling $420.00. Those fees are : Account ending in : payment posted $35.00 fee applied posted $35.00 fee applied Account ending in : posted $35.00 fee applied . posted $35.00 fee applied * posted $35.00 fee applied $35.00 fee applied posted $35.00 fee applied NJ posted $35.00 fee applied posted $35.00 fee applied posted $35.00 fee applied posted $35.00 fee applied posted $35.00 fee applied That is $420.00 in overdraft fees identified by Wells Fargo . Wells Fargos handling of this matter also appears to raise UDAAP concerns under the Consumer Financial Protection Act. The CFPB may prevent a covered person from engaging in an unfair, deceptive, or abusive act or practice in connection with a consumer financial product or service, and it is unlawful for a covered person to engage in an unfair, deceptive, or abusive act or practice. 12 U.S.C. 5531 ( a ), 5536 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( B ). An act or practice is unfair where it causes or is likely to cause substantial injury to consumers, the injury is not reasonably avoidable by consumers, and the injury is not outweighed by countervailing benefits to consumers or competition. 12 U.S.C. 5531 ( c ). Here, Wells Fargo reversed provisional credit, retained overdraft fees, and provided only a conclusory explanation rather than a transparent, evidence-based explanation of how it determined the disputed transactions were authorized. Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ) requires clear disclosure of credit card terms and any material modifications. Regulation Z implements TILA ; governs disclosure obligations for credit card accounts including workout and hardship arrangements. Consumer Financial Protection Act UDAAP provisions prohibiting unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices in connection with consumer financial products. -- - . RELIEF REQUESTED . narrative: American Express Dispute . On , I paid $2600.00 for garage door repairs : two torsion springs, one cable drum, and labor. The parts alone were billed at $2000.00. Those same parts retail for under $120.00 total. This submission explains the overcharge and the law violations that accompanied it. Factual Background : I found the company through what appeared to be a listing for a local garage-door service. It was late at night and cold, so we needed an immediate fix. A technician named arrived and examined my garage door. He told me the springs needed replacing and mentioned they would cost about $350.00 each. He provide no written estimate or a form to choose between written and oral estimates, and he failed to disclose my rights under law. When the work was done, presented the bill : $750.00 per spring ( not $350.00 ), plus $550.00 for a drum, plus $370.00 labor, plus a $75.00 card fee. Total : $2500.00 before tip. I paid because I needed my garage door to function and felt I had no practical alternative at that point. It was late at night, he was a bit intimidating, and I wanted him out of my house. left me a box for one of the torsion springs.There was no paperwork whatsoeverno specifications, no warranty, nothing. And my internet research has failed to identify the manufacturer. This is a generic product, probably inferior, and misrepresented it as top of the line. The Overcharge : The invoice describes the springs as " New American springs '' with electrophoretic coating. On , a pair of electrophoresis-coated torsion springs with cycle ratingsincluding winding barssells for $40.00 to $80.00 ; the merchant charged $1500.00 for the pair. The drum is simpler. sells garage door cable drums for about $8.00. prices are similar. , a professional repair company, advertises complete drum replacementparts and laborfor $200.00 to $300.00 ( see ). But the merchant charged me $550.00 for the part alone.Adding reasonable labor ( $300000.00 ) to fair parts pricing ( $75000.00 ), this repair should have cost $400.00 to $550.00. I paid $2500.00. Violations of Law : The Consumer Sales Practices Act, R.C. 1345.01, et seq. ( the CSPA ), requires suppliers in these circumstances to do two pertinent things that the vendor here did not do : ( 1 ) provide a written estimate ( or obtain a written waiver of that right ) ; and ( 2 ) refrain from unreasonably overcharging. Failure to do these things warrants rescission of the transaction and a full refund of the funds paid, plus treble economic damages and attorney fees. In addition, the vendor provided fraudulent and deceptive information about the supposed warranty on the parts. 1. Failure to Provide Proper ( and Accurate ) Estimate : Administrative Code 109:4-3-05 is one of the regulations that implements the CSPA for home repairs costing more than $25.00. It requires the repair company to do two things at the initial face-to-face contact, before starting any work : ( 1 ) orally inform the consumer of the right to receive a written or oral estimate, and ( 2 ) provide a form allowing the consumer to choose. did neither. He did not inform me of any rights. He did not provide any form. He started working and presented the price afterward. I understand the merchant may argue that an oral estimate was given. Two problems with that. First, no form was provided for me to elect an oral estimatethe regulation requires the form regardless of which type of estimate the consumer chooses. Second, even if 's casual mention of " about $350.00 '' qualified as an oral estimate, the final charge of $750.00 per spring exceeded it by 114 %. Under OAC 109:4-3-05, the final bill can not exceed the estimate by more than 10 % without prior approval. I gave no such approval. 2. Overcharges : R.C. 1345.03 ( B ) ( 2 ) makes it a deceptive act or practice to charge a price substantially in excess of the price at which similar property or services were readily obtainable in similar consumer transactions by like consumer. The enormous discrepancy between the market prices and the prices I was charged for the torsion springs and drum speaks for itself. . Fake Warranty : The invoice states 20 years of warranty. The merchant 's own Terms & Conditions, accessible via link on the receipt, limit the warranty to 30 days on labor onlyno parts coverage. But the warranty is obviously useless, because I have no way to identify, much less contact, either the manufacturer or ( at this point ) the vendor. The Scam Pattern : This company fits the profile of a well-documented national fraud. In , the Serving warned consumers about garage-door-repair scams after a , , resident reported a nearly identical experience : a company found via sponsored ads, no physical address, an number that changes every time you look it up, and inflated charges for parts.1 The merchant here has no physical addressnone appears on the invoice or receipt. The contact email is a account ( ). The phone number is an toll-free line. Payment was processed through in , third-party processor commonly used in these operations. The company name, , is generic and does not appear to be a registered business. News investigations from and the describe the same pattern : fake listings with stolen photos, calls routed to out-of-state call centers, unlicensed technicians dispatched as gig workers, no estimates provided, and parts marked up by 1,000 % or more. ( ) Contact History : After I disputed the charge, the merchant contacted me twice : once by text and once by voice call. On , someone named sent a text message asking if I had concerns. I responded the same day with a clear explanation of the problem : You violated law by not providing an accurate written estimate before the work was done and then you overcharged me significantly for parts that are not even name-brand. The phone call followed and was aggressive and unproductive. I had already submitted the dispute to American Express by this time, so for my comfort and security I blocked the number. Its unreasonable to anticipate that a business that would engage in this sort of fraud and deception would then come to the negotiating table in good faith. And, indeed, in recent days I have tried calling the number again from a different phone ( so the merchant would not see it was me ) ; the phone number no longer connected to a garage-door-repair service but instead has a generic message of unavailability. What the Merchant Should Be Able to Produce : If the merchant 's position is legitimate, it should be able to produce three things. First, invoices from its supplier showing what it actually paid for the springs and drum. If those parts cost anywhere near $2000.00, the invoices will show it. Second, a signed form in which I elected an oral estimate and waived my right to a written oneas required by OAC 109:4-3-05. Third, documentation of the 20 years of warranty advertised on the invoice, which should exist as a written warranty document rather than a contradiction buried in online terms and conditions. And I want the name and contact information for the manufacturer. I expect the merchant can produce none of these. Summary : I was charged $2000.00 for parts worth approximately $100.00. The company violated estimate disclosure requirements. The final bill exceeded even the informal oral quote by more than 100 %. The merchant operates without a physical address, uses a account and third-party payment processor, and matches the documented profile of garage door repair fraud. narrative: Opening Statement This complaint concerns a foreclosure proceeding in which the mortgage servicer relied on a vendor declaration stating that a Notice of Trustee Sale was posted at my property. Documentation from the entity responsible for managing access to the gated community where the property is located confirms that the posting agent never requested entry and never accessed the community. Complaint Summary This complaint concerns defective foreclosure notice procedures and inaccurate vendor declarations used in connection with foreclosure activity involving the property located in , . A posting affidavit prepared by a foreclosure vendor states that the Notice of Trustee Sale was posted at the property on . However, documentation from the Community Services District, which manages the controlled-access entrance to the community where the property is located, confirms that no process server or posting agent requested entry into the community on that date. Because the property is located inside a gated community that requires access authorization to enter, the posting agent could not have reached the property without requesting entry. This raises concerns that the declaration stating the notice was posted at the property may be inaccurate. Evidence Supporting This Complaint Vendor Posting Declaration A document titled Proof of Notice of Trustee Sale Posting prepared by the foreclosure vendor indicates that the Notice of Trustee Sale was posted on at the property address. The declaration indicates that the notice was posted at locations including the front door, gate, or garage of the property. Community Access Records Community Services District reviewed its records and confirmed the following regarding the date of the alleged posting : No process server or posting agent requested entry into the community No authorization for entry was granted No identification of an individual serving foreclosure documents was recorded No administrative record exists showing entry by a posting agent Because the property is located within a controlled-access gated community, entry authorization is required in order to physically reach the property. These records indicate that no such entry occurred. Documentation of Gate Posting The district further confirmed that on , an individual approached the community entrance gate and placed papers on the gate without requesting authorization to enter the community. The entrance gate serves more than homes and is located approximately mile from the property. Placing papers on the entrance gate is not equivalent to posting notice at the property itself. Material Discrepancy in Foreclosure Documentation The vendor declaration states that the Notice of Trustee Sale was posted at the property address. However, the access records maintained by the entity responsible for managing entry into the gated community confirm that the posting agent never requested entry and therefore never reached the property. This creates a significant discrepancy between the foreclosure vendors declaration and the independent records documenting access to the community. Consumer Protection Concerns Mortgage servicers remain responsible for the conduct of third-party vendors acting on their behalf during foreclosure proceedings. When foreclosure activity relies on vendor declarations, the servicer must ensure that those declarations are accurate and supported by verifiable documentation. Proceeding with foreclosure activity based on inaccurate vendor declarations raises concerns regarding unfair or deceptive servicing practices and inadequate oversight of foreclosure vendors. Requested Investigation I respectfully request that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau investigate whether : 1. The foreclosure vendor submitted an inaccurate declaration regarding the posting of the Notice of Trustee Sale 2. The mortgage servicer relied on vendor documentation that conflicts with independent access records 3. Adequate oversight of foreclosure vendors was conducted 4. The foreclosure process relied on defective statutory notice procedures Requested Resolution I request that the servicer : Explain how the notice could have been posted at the property when the posting agent never accessed the community Produce the documentation supporting the alleged posting of the Notice of Trustee Sale on , including the vendor work order, service logs, and any photographs taken by the posting vendor showing where the notice was posted Confirm whether foreclosure activity relied on inaccurate vendor declarations Suspend foreclosure activity until this discrepancy is fully investigated Supporting Documentation The following documents support this complaint : Posting affidavit / proof of posting prepared by the foreclosure vendor Written confirmation from the Community Services District regarding access records and entry procedures Potential Systemic Concern The discrepancy between the foreclosure vendors declaration and the independent access records maintained by the Community Services District raises concerns that inaccurate posting declarations may have been submitted in connection with foreclosure proceedings. If a foreclosure vendor is submitting declarations stating that notices were posted at properties when access records show the vendor never entered the community where the property is located, this raises broader concerns regarding the accuracy of foreclosure documentation and the adequacy of servicer oversight of third-party vendors. I respectfully request that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau determine whether similar practices may have occurred in other foreclosure proceedings involving this servicer or its vendors. Additional Context The documentation from the Community Services District dated has also been submitted as Exhibit C in pending court filings related to this matter. The court has not yet issued its order regarding those filings. Because this documentation is already part of the evidentiary record before the court, the discrepancy between the foreclosure vendors declaration and the community access records is currently under review. I am providing the same documentation to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau so that the accuracy of the foreclosure notice procedures and the servicers oversight of its foreclosure vendors can also be evaluated. Because the documentation referenced in this complaint is already part of pending court filings and directly contradicts the foreclosure vendors declaration regarding the posting of the Notice of Trustee Sale, I respectfully request that Wells Fargo conduct an immediate review of the foreclosure file to ensure that the foreclosure process has relied on accurate documentation and proper statutory notice procedures.

Card skimming, phishing, credential theft, and dark web data breaches allow criminals to steal and use card credentials without ever physically possessing the card. narrative: CFPB COMPLAINT / FORMAL DISPUTE ESCALATION Company : American Express National Bank Consumer : : , AR Accounts : ( ending / ) ; Business Gold ( ending ) Issue : Regulation Z Billing Error Investigation and Procedural Compliance COMPLAINT NARRATIVE This complaint concerns American Express 's repeated closure of documented billing disputes based solely on a " '' timing assertion, without addressing certified written notices, merchant coding irregularities, or previously established knowledge of the disputed activity. The issue presented is not whether a charge was processed through the payment network, but whether American Express complied with its investigation obligations under the Fair Credit Billing Act ( 15 U.S.C. 1666 ) and Regulation Z ( 12 C.F.R. 1026.13 ). American Express has issued multiple form letters stating : " Because this dispute was reported more than 60 days after your statement date, we weren't able to investigate it. '' This statement mischaracterizes the regulatory framework. I. THE 60-DAY PROVISION DOES NOT ELIMINATE INVESTIGATIVE AUTHORITY 12 C.F.R. 1026.13 ( b ) ( 1 ) defines when certain statutory protections are automatically triggered upon timely written notice. It does not prohibit investigation outside 60 days, nor does it remove creditor authority to evaluate billing errors. The repeated use of a categorical " unable to investigate '' position suggests a procedural policy rather than an individualized review of the dispute. The complaint requests CFPB review of whether American Express is : Treating the provision as a jurisdictional bar, Or using it to decline review despite documented written notice and knowledge. II. EARLY KNOWLEDGE AND REPEATED WRITTEN NOTICE American Express received written notice of these disputed transactions in early . Additional certified correspondence followed. Once a creditor receives notice of a potential billing error, Regulation Z requires a reasonable investigation and written explanation of findings ( 1026.13 ( f ) ). Despite this knowledge trigger, subsequent dispute closures in relied solely on the language without addressing : The certified mail receipts, The evidence submitted, Or the timeline of prior notice. The concern is whether internal records reflecting earlier notice were considered before closing the disputes. III. MCC MISCODING AND STATEMENT ACCURACY The merchants involved ( , ) operate as sweepstakes-gaming platforms. The transactions were processed under merchant category codes ( MCCs ) that did not reflect the restricted MCC 7995 typically associated with gambling activity. Improper MCC coding and obscured trade names may constitute billing errors under : 12 C.F.R. 1026.13 ( a ) ( 3 ) ( incorrect amount or description ) 12 C.F.R. 1026.13 ( a ) ( 6 ) ( statement inaccuracies ) These issues are independent of whether an authorization code was generated. The periodic statement must accurately reflect the nature of the transaction. The complaint requests review of whether American Express evaluated the coding discrepancy as part of its investigation. IV. FAILURE TO ADDRESS CERTIFIED MAIL NOTICE Formal written notices were transmitted via certified mail consistent with FCBA requirements. American Express 's dispute-closure letters do not reference : The certified mail tracking, The dates of delivery, Or the contents of the written submissions. Section 1026.13 ( f ) requires a written explanation of findings after investigation. A generic reference to " 60 days '' does not address the substance of a written billing error notice. The concern is whether the investigation obligation was bypassed rather than fulfilled. V. DIGITAL WALLET PROVISIONING IS NOT DISPOSITIVE If reliance is placed on Apple Pay provisioning or the presence of an authorization code, that information alone does not establish that : The statement was accurate, The transaction description was proper, Or that no billing error exists. Provisioning demonstrates device enrollment - not necessarily accurate merchant classification or legal authority of the underlying charge. VI. INCONSISTENT APPLICATION OF THE 60-DAY POSITION American Express has , in prior instances, investigated disputes submitted beyond days. If the window is discretionary in practice, it should not function as a categorical bar in this instance. This raises a compliance consistency concern appropriate for supervisory review.

All flight segments in a multi-segment itinerary must have this limited fare inventory available, which dramatically reduces usable options. Travel must be round-trip and completed before expiration, further reducing flexibility. Alaska residents face additional practical barriers due to routing limitations and limited flight inventory from smaller markets. The certificate often can not be used during peak or typical vacation travel periods when most consumers would naturally expect to travel. Many consumers, including myself, experience repeated failed searches and ultimately risk certificate expiration due to lack of qualifying flights. While these limitations are disclosed in the fine print, they are not presented with comparable prominence to the headline marketing message. The marketing creates a strong impression of a broadly usable annual companion ticket, while the actual redemption process is highly constrained and difficult for many consumers to use successfully. This creates a material gap between the perceived value used to justify the annual fee and the practical usability of the benefit. I respectfully request that this promotion be reviewed for potentially misleading marketing practices, particularly regarding : The prominence and clarity of limitations The real-world usability of the advertised benefit Whether the average consumer would reasonably understand the redemption difficulty before applying for the card Thank you for your time and for reviewing this concern.

The central issue is not whether a timing concept exists, but how American Express has applied it. American Express has relied on the rationale to deny certain disputes while simultaneously crediting or actively investigating other transactions from the same merchants and time periods that are equal toor older thanthe denied transactions. As documented in the attached exhibits, transaction age has not been the controlling factor. Instead, materially similar transactions have received materially different outcomes. Once American Express elected to investigate and credit transactions beyond the asserted window, it effectively abandoned any claim that age alone serves as a strict eligibility bar. Having exercised discretion to review and credit older transactions, American Express can not coherently invoke timing as a rigid rule to summarily deny other disputes involving the same merchants, similar dates, and the same dispute posture. narrative: This complaint highlights a statutory ambiguity that allows creditors to continue coercive conduct post-petition while claiming technical compliance. The attached letter explains why clearer statutory or supervisory guidance is necessary. This complaint concerns ongoing, systemic issues in American Express post-bankruptcy account management practices that reveal a significant gap between the intent of the Bankruptcy Codes automatic stay and how modern, automated financial systems are in practice. After filing for bankruptcy and providing repeated notice, American Express continued to display, transmit, and communicate pre-petition balances through its internal systems and live agents. Although certain automated payment features were partially suppressed, core balance information remained visible and was verbally conveyed by customer service representatives, functioning in substance as a continuation of collection activity. American Express has assertedboth directly and implicitlythat these disclosures are merely informational and not acts to collect a debt. This position exploits statutory ambiguity in 11 U.S.C. 362 ( a ) ( 6 ), which broadly prohibits acts to collect but does not expressly address modern digital account interfaces, countdown mechanisms, or live-agent balance confirmations that replicate the same coercive effect as traditional collection efforts. The attached advocacy memorandum explains why clearer statutory or supervisory guidance is necessary. Without specificity, large creditors are able to design systems that technically comply with narrow interpretations of the law while functionally defeating its consumer-protective purpose. The burden then falls on individual debtors to litigate whether each display, prompt, or communication constitutes an act to collectan outcome that undermines uniform enforcement and judicial efficiency. This complaint is submitted not only to address the conduct experienced in this case, but also to highlight a recurring, industry-wide problem affecting thousands of bankruptcy filers annually. Regulatory attention is warranted to assess whether existing guidance sufficiently addresses automated collection practices in the bankruptcy context and whether additional clarification or enforcement action is necessary.

Authorization : The bank executes OC-10 documents, granting a security interest to the Fed ( Federal Reserve Banks ). Grant of Power : The bank executes a Power of Attorney, allowing the Fed to " negotiate '' the citizen 's instrument ( , , p. ). Custody : The bank marks its internal records, identifying the note as " subject exclusively to the Banks [ Fed 's ] written instructions '' ( , , p. ). Monetization : The Fed issues credit or notes to the bank 's " Account '' based on the lendable value of the collateral ( Federal Reserve Board, ). Maintenance : The bank must remove " matured, paid, or past due '' loans from the pledge, confirming the collateral 's dynamic nature ( , , p. ). The analysis identifies a zero-sum transaction on the public ledger ( 59 Stat. 237, ). Any attempt to assert a " residual debt '' against the citizen fails for lack of statutory backing, as the " tender '' was already accepted at par to satisfy the issuance of the currency ( 12 U.S.C. 414, 2025 ). The impact on the citizen is the use of their private credit to fund the public banking system without a corresponding discharge of the alleged private debt ( Federal Reserve Board, ). Fiduciary Trust and Custodial Obligations in BIC Arrangements The critical legal pivot occurs within the " Borrower-in-Custody '' ( BIC ) arrangement, which fundamentally alters the bank 's ownership rights over the citizen 's instrument ( , ). Under the BIC arrangement, the bank is authorized to " retain possession of the Collateral, '' but only as an agent for the Federal Reserve Bank , ). The bank no longer owns the note in its own right ; it holds it " in trust '' as a custodian for the official principal, which is the Federal Reserve Bank ( , ). This custodial relationship is a conclusion of law derived from Operating Circular No. 10, where the bank transfers and assigns to the Federal Reserve Bank a continuing security interest in and on the Collateral ( Federal Reserve Banks, ). This " transfer and assignment '' means the " bundle of rights '' associated with ownership has been legally moved to the Federal Reserve ( Uniform Commercial Code [ UCC ] 9-203, ). The bank 's remaining role is strictly defined as a " Custodian '' under the " Custody Agreement '' found in Appendix A of OC-10 ( ). The legal implications of this custodial status are governed by the law of Agency, where the Agent ( the bank ) must act for the Principal ( the Federal Reserve ) and is subject to the Principal 's exclusive control ( Restatement ( Third ) of Agency, ). The BIC Guidelines explicitly state that BIC-held collateral must be subject exclusively to the Banks [ Fed 's ] written instructions ( FRBSF, ). Actionable Unjust Enrichment via UCC Remedies A general claim of " unjust enrichment '' is often dismissed in academic discourse as an equitable remedy that is unavailable when a contract exists ( , ). However, by linking this claim to specific UCC remedies, it becomes a statutory cause of action ( , ). The primary mechanism for this is a " Demand for Accounting '' under UCC 9-210 ( UCC 9-210, ). By issuing a formal Request for Accounting, the Citizen Borrower demands a line-item breakdown of how the " lendable value '' or collateral was applied within the financial management system ( UCC 9-210 ). If the institution has accepted the asset but has not adjusted the liability on the ledger, the " unjust enrichment '' is no longer a vague concept ; it is a documented failure to account for collateral under secured transactions law ( UCC 9-210, ). This forces the institution to either admit the application of the collateral or risk statutory penalties for failing to provide an accurate accounting of the " public trust '' assets they manage on behalf of the Citizen Borrower , ).

narrative: I am submitting this complaint regarding American Expresss handling and closure of my dispute for unauthorized charges. Unauthorized charges began appearing on my American Express card in and continued for several months, totaling $14000.00. This credit card is used solely for travel purposes, which is why it is not reviewed frequently. When I eventually discovered the charges, I learned they were made by my son using an old phone that still contained stored payment credentials. American Express closed my case after determining that I authorized the charges because I allowed my minor son to use the old phone. This conclusion is flawed and not aligned with consumer protection principles or fair billing standards. I did not authorize my son to use my credit card or to make any financial transactions. I only permitted limited, non-financial use of a device, such as watching videos. Permission to access a device does not constitute express or implied authorization to use stored payment credentials or to conduct financial transactions. Authorization requires knowing and intentional consent to payment activity, which I did not provide. The charges were made by my son, a minor who lacks legal capacity to enter binding contracts. I did not approve, ratify, or knowingly permit these transactions. Treating device access as equivalent to payment authorization ignores the legal distinction between access and authority, particularly where a minor is involved. Several procedural concerns occurred during this process : Misclassification and routing loop American Express stated that the dispute was reviewed by the billing dispute department and then routed back to fraud, where it was closed. This resulted in no department making a substantive determination regarding authorization, and the case was closed due to internal routing rules rather than a fair evaluation. Inconsistent reasoning by representatives Representatives stated that I was responsible for my old device, implying that responsibility for device security equates to authorization of financial transactions. This reasoning conflates assumed risk with consent and shifts liability without establishing that authorization was knowingly given. Procedural convenience over fairness The case was closed under a narrow fraud definition after a prolonged investigation, despite the fact that this involved unauthorized charges made by a minor. This outcome appears procedurally convenient rather than a fair application of consumer billing protections. Delay causing loss of recovery opportunity The investigation took over a month to conclude, during which time potential recovery options were diminished. Not a single charge was refunded, despite the significant total amount and the circumstances involved. At no point did American Express allege that I personally made the charges or acted dishonestly. Instead, the denial was based on internal policy assumptions that device access equals payment authorization. This standard is unreasonable and inconsistent with the principle that authorization must be intentional, knowing, and specific to financial transactions. I respectfully request that the CFPB review whether American Express properly applied authorization standards and fair billing protections, and whether closing this dispute based on device access rather than explicit payment consent is consistent with consumer law and fair credit practices.

narrative: This complaint is submitted as a supplemental and updated complaint following a prior CFPB filing regarding Wells Fargo Home Mortgages handling of our loss-mitigation application and foreclosure proceedings. Despite prior regulatory notice and court involvement, Wells Fargo has issued conflicting and irreconcilable communications regarding the status of the loan, foreclosure posture, and HUD involvement, creating ongoing risk of wrongful foreclosure and depriving us of due process. Background On , we submitted a complete Mortgage Assistance / Loss Mitigation Application, including all required documentation. Wells Fargo failed to provide any written acknowledgment, completeness determination, approval, or denial, as required by 12 C.F.R. 1024.41 ( c ) ( d ). Wells Fargo later claimed documents were sent to an attorney on file, despite the borrowers being self-represented, with prior counsel formally withdrawn. No documents were ever served directly on us. Foreclosure and HUD-Related Communications While loss mitigation remained unresolved, Wells Fargo scheduled foreclosure activity, raising dual-tracking concerns under 12 C.F.R. 1024.41 ( g ). On , foreclosure counsel , acting on behalf of Wells Fargo, issued a Notice to Occupants of Pending Acquisition referencing a HUD/FHA case number and advising that title was expected to transfer to Wells Fargo and potentially to HUD following foreclosure Tricey House Document ( 1 ). The same correspondence included HUD Occupied Conveyance procedures, forms, and instructions applicable only after foreclosure and conveyance, including : Requests for HUD approval to remain in the property Conditions for temporary continued occupancy Employment verification and rental qualification requirements Document back page These communications represent that foreclosure and HUD conveyance are proceeding or imminent, and that the borrowers rights are limited to post-foreclosure occupancy determinations. Conflicting Wells Fargo Representations days later, on , Wells Fargo issued a separate letter stating that a mortgage assistance application was under review, that additional time was needed, and that loss mitigation options were still being evaluated. That letter did not disclose : Whether the application was complete or incomplete What documents were missing Whether foreclosure activity had been paused That foreclosure counsel was simultaneously issuing HUD conveyance notices As a result, Wells Fargo and its agents issued materially conflicting representations : One set of communications treats foreclosure and HUD conveyance as imminent and unavoidable ; Another represents that loss mitigation review remains ongoing. These positions can not both be true. Regulatory Concerns This conduct raises serious concerns regarding : 12 C.F.R. 1024.41 ( c ), ( d ), and ( g ) failure to properly process loss-mitigation applications and prohibition on dual tracking RESPA servicing requirements for accurate, consistent, and transparent borrower communications Potential misrepresentation to HUD and to borrowers regarding foreclosure status Deprivation of due process and inability to exercise appeal or review rights Issuing HUD Occupied Conveyance materials while simultaneously claiming loss mitigation is under review is misleading, prejudicial, and incompatible with Regulation X. Recent Escalation On , we submitted a Qualified Written Request ( QWR ) seeking clarification, correction of servicing errors, and reconciliation of these conflicting communications. A HUD complaint has been submitted concurrently regarding potential FHA servicing violations, including inconsistent representations regarding foreclosure and HUD conveyance. As of the date of this complaint, Wells Fargo has not reconciled these conflicts or provided a clear, compliant explanation of the loans true status.
