narrative: Hello, My name is , I am submitting this complaint because American Express ( AMEX ) has furnished two business credit card accounts to my personal consumer credit reports as if they were individual consumer obligations, resulting in significant and ongoing damage to my personal credit profile. This is a misclassification error, and the reporting is inaccurate under FCRA 602 ( a ), 623 ( a ) ( 1 ), and reporting standards. These accounts are commercial accounts for my business, . The AMEX statements clearly identify : disclosures and terms Business customer service channels Business credit limits Business address printed directly on the statements These documents confirm that both accounts are commercial products. However, AMEX furnished these accounts to Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion as : Account Type : Consumer Credit Card Responsibility : Individual Status : Consumer Charge-Off Payment History : Personal derogatory history Loan Type : Personal revolving account This information is factually incorrect and misleading. report shows the AMEX account coded as : Responsibility : Individual Account Type : Credit Card Status : Charged Off ( $14000.00 written off ) Past due balance and derogatory consumer historXXXX report lists both AMEX accounts as : Individual Account Revolving Consumer Credit Card Charge-Off Multiple derogatory months These entries are not accurate, because the debts are business obligations and not personal consumer credit. Furnishing them as personal charge-offs has caused : Significant score reduction Incorrect derogatory payment history Incorrect utilization calculations Ongoing negative updates each month Loss of personal and business credit opportunities I want to emphasize that I am not disputing the underlying business debt. I am disputing the pattern of misreporting and the unfair harm caused by AMEXs inaccurate furnishing practices. When this issue first occurred, I did not understand how the reporting system worked and assumed the bureaus would correct the mistake. Only after researching the issue myself did I discover thousands of similar complaints filed against AMEX across multiple years describing the same conductmisclassification, reporting business accounts as personal, and failing to correct inaccurate information. In addition to this CFPB complaint, I am preparing a formal letter to Congress because the public data shows that consumers nationwide have been repeatedly harmed in the same way, year after year, without meaningful enforcement or systemic correction. Furnishers should be held to the same accuracy standards that consumers are held to, especially when misclassification of commercial accounts as personal obligations causes significant financial harm. Stronger oversight and enforcement is needed to prevent these issues from repeating for future consumers. ======== There is a structural gap in the credit-reporting system that allows this harm to occur and continue. Today : The investigation process is slow ( often 30 days or more ). The credit-scoring engine is instant. These systems do not communicate with each other. Because of this separation, inaccurate data furnished by AMEX is allowed to still : Continue updating Continue refreshing Continue being treated as verified Continue lowering credit scores even while the account is under an active dispute and supposedly under review. From a consumer-protection standpoint, there is no logical or fair reason that a disputed account especially under investigation should continue to harm a consumers score in real time. This creates unavoidable and ongoing consumer injury because : Consumers are penalized before accuracy is confirmed. Incorrect information remains visible and continues to generate negative scoring impacts. Derogatory codes continue accumulating in the background. The system defaults to protecting the furnishers data stream rather than protecting the consumer. This design flaw means that even when a consumer identifies a serious misclassification ( such as a business account incorrectly reported as personal ) and disputes it, the damage continues throughout the investigation period. This is what is happening in my case : the incorrect AMEX charge-off is still refreshing during the dispute, and my credit score continues to be harmed while accuracy is being examined.

narrative: SUMMARY OF COMPLAINT Wells Fargo Bank , N.A . has engaged in a systemic pattern of disregarding state law and federal bankruptcy requirements when processing legal orders against business accounts. Specifically, Wells Fargo seized approximately $32000.00 from an active debtor-in-possession ( DIP ) account based on an undomesticated New York judgment, without providing advance notice as required by Texas law, and without verifying compliance with the Bankruptcy Code 's automatic stay and plan confirmation order. The bank 's own policy documents and counsel admissions demonstrate that Wells Fargo knowingly operates under a practice of willful disregard for state domestication/notice requirements and federal bankruptcy protections, choosing to act on legal process " regardless of how and where it is served '' and taking " no stance '' on whether such process is legally valid. This conduct has caused severe financial harm to the business, resulting in : Inability to make court-ordered plan payments due Lapse of general liability insurance Cascade of consequential business defaults Threat of plan failure and forced liquidation DETAILED COMPLAINT NARRATIVE Background : DIP Account Status and Bankruptcy Protections is operating as a confirmed of the Bankruptcy Code in the Southern District of Texas ( Case ). The business has a confirmed plan and is in active performance of all obligations. The seized account is clearly labeled as a " DIP Account '' and is account property of the bankruptcy estate, protected by : 1. 11 U.S.C. 362 The automatic stay, which prohibits creditors from enforcing judgments against estate property 2. 11 U.S.C. 1141 ( d ) ( 1 ) The plan confirmation order, which permanently injuncts claims not discharged by the plan 3. The Confirmation Order issued by the bankruptcy court, which injected all creditors from pursuing claims outside the plan framework The Undomesticated New York Judgment The underlying garnishment was based on a New York state court judgment entered in ( a default judgment obtained without proper service or notice to the debtor ). This judgment was never domesticated in Texas before Wells Fargo acted on it. Texas law requires : Under Texas Civil Procedure , foreign judgments must be domesticated ( filed and recognized ) in Texas before a creditor can use local remedies like garnishment Under Texas Finance Code 59.004, banks processing garnishments must verify that the legal process is properly issued and, under garnishment law, that the debtor has received notice Wells Fargo disregarded both requirements. Wells Fargo 's Systemic Policy of Willful Disregard Wells Fargo 's own documents reveal a deliberate policy choice to avoid due diligence on legal process : 1. Deposit Account Agreement Page 39 ( " Blanket Authorization '' ) The agreement states : " We may accept and act on any legal process we believe to be valid regardless of how and where it is served, including if process is served in locations, states, or jurisdictions other than where the account was opened or where the account, property, or records are located. '' This language reserves Wells Fargo 's discretion to act on legal process without regard to state domestication or procedural requirements. The phrase " we believe to be valid '' creates a subjective standard that shifts the bank 's incentive away from actually verifying validity. 2. No Notice Policy The same agreement states : " We may, but are not required to, provide notice of legal process relating to your accounts. '' Combined with the blanket authorization, this creates a policy incentive for Wells Fargo to act on legal process first and avoid notice to the account holder, thereby preventing the debtor from raising defenses before funds are seized. 3. Counsel Admission of " No Stance '' ( Email ) In written correspondence, Wells Fargo 's legal counsel explicitly stated that the bank : " takes no stance on the propriety of the judgment or garnishment '' and " simply complies with the New York restraint. '' This admission confirms that Wells Fargo made a conscious choice NOT to evaluate whether the judgment was properly domesticated or whether the garnishment was legally valid under Texas law. Instead, the bank chose mechanical compliance with an out-of-state order, despite holding clear knowledge that : The account is labeled a DIP account The debtor is in active bankruptcy The judgment was never domesticated in Texas State law and federal law both require verification before seizure How This Conduct Violates Consumer Protection Standards 1. Willful Stay Violation ( 11 U.S.C. 362 ) o The account is estate property protected by the automatic stay o Wells Fargo 's seizure, made with knowledge of the bankruptcy filing, violates the stay o This is not a case of mistaken identity or error ; the bank had explicit notice and chose to act anyway 2. Failure to Verify Legal Process Validity ( Texas Finance Code 59.004 & 63.001 et seq. ) o Texas garnishment law requires the bank to verify that garnishment is properly issued and that debtor notice requirements are met o Wells Fargo 's policy of taking " no stance '' on the legal validity of out-of-state process violates this standard o The bank 's own counsel admission proves this was a policy choice, not an error 3. Violation of State Domestication Requirements ( Texas C.P.C. 35.003 ) o Foreign judgments can not be enforced in Texas through garnishment until domesticated o Wells Fargo acted on a non-domesticated judgment, making the seizure improper under state law o This was not an isolated mistake ; the pattern documents show this is how Wells Fargo systematically processes out-of-state legal process 4. Deceptive Financial Practices ( 15 U.S.C. 1681 et seq. & Texas DTPA ) o The blanket authorization language ( page 39 ) is drafted to disguise the bank 's policy of avoiding due diligence on legal process o Consumers reasonably expect that banks will comply with state domestication requirements and provide notice before seizing accounts o Wells Fargo 's policy is designed to shift all risk to the consumer while reserving the bank 's right to act on invalid legal process Financial and Consequential Harm The seizure of $32000.00 on , created an immediate cascade of harm : Plan Payment Default : The plan required a $9500.00 payment due . Details of the Issue In , I placed a lock on my Wells Fargo credit card, which should have prevented any new transactions. Shortly afterward, I was incarcerated and did not have access to my card or my account. When I was released, my account balance was significantly higher than expected. A collection agent later contacted me and demanded payment of over $1000.00 as a settlement. I paid it in full. Despite this, Wells Fargo has reported negative information on my credit report, including late payment and settlement notations. I submitted a formal written request to Wells Fargo demanding : A complete transaction history from through the date the account was closed. The card lock log, showing dates, duration, and attempted use. Proof of how Wells Fargo calculated the debt prior to sending it to collections. Documentation of payments made to the collection agency. Verification supporting all negative credit reporting. Wells Fargo failed to provide these records. Without these records, the accuracy of the information being reported to credit bureaus can not be verified, and the continued reporting violates FCRA. How This Violates Federal Law Wells Fargos conduct violates multiple FCRA provisions : 1. Failure to conduct a reasonable investigation 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( b ). Wells Fargo did not investigate or verify the disputed information despite my written dispute. 2. Reporting inaccurate or unverifiable information 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ). Wells Fargo continues to report late payments and settlement data even though the underlying transactions remain unverified. . Failure to provide documentation used in credit reporting. Under FCRA and related case law, furnishers must be able to substantiate negative information. Supporting Case Law I cite the following federal appellate decisions, which clearly define furnishers duties : ) held that a furnisher can not refuse to conduct an investigation by labeling a consumer dispute as frivolous. Once notified of a dispute, investigation is mandatory. ( ) The ruled that disputes involving objectively and readily verifiable information must be investigated by furnishers, rejecting the notion that legal issues excuse compliance. The court held that an FCRA plaintiff may proceed where information furnished is inaccurate or materially misleading, meaning it can adversely affect credit decisions. Negative reporting without proof of legitimacy meets this standard. ( ) precedent, information is actionable under FCRA if it is patently incorrect or materially misleading. Reporting late payments based on unverified transactions fits this test. FTC and CFPB joint findings ( ) Regulators have stated that furnishers must investigate and can not dismiss consumer disputes by claiming they involve legal questions. Harm Suffered Wells Fargos failure to investigate, failure to provide documentation, and inaccurate reporting have harmed my creditworthiness, caused credit score reduction, and created long-term financial consequences. I can not correct these issues without the documentation Wells Fargo is withholding.

If bank employees falsely claim to be executives when contacting customers, the conduct can rise to several criminal and regulatory violations, depending on intent and impact. A. False Pretenses / Fraud ( 18 U.S.C. 1343 or 1344 ) If an employee falsely represents their position to gain something of value such as information, payment, or leverage in a negotiation that can constitute : Wire fraud ( 18 U.S.C. 1343 ) if done via phone, email, or electronic means ; or Bank fraud ( 18 U.S.C. 1344 ) if the deception involves the banks operations or a customers account. Penalties : Up to 30 years in prison and fines up to {>= $1,000,000} for bank fraud. B. Impersonation of an Officer or Employee of a Bank ( 18 U.S.C. 912 / 709 ) These laws make it a crime to falsely represent oneself as a bank officer, agent, or employee to obtain something of value or to mislead others. 18 U.S.C. 709 specifically prohibits using the name or title of a bank or officer with intent to deceive. Example : A mid-level employee emails a customer claiming to be a Vice President of Credit to intimidate them into making a payment. 18 U.S.C. 912 applies to impersonation of federal officers, but 709 covers bank officer impersonation. Penalty : Federal misdemeanor up to 1 year imprisonment and/or fines, and can escalate if part of broader fraud. C. Conspiracy ( 18 U.S.C. 371 ) If multiple employees coordinate this misrepresentation, they can be charged with conspiracy to commit fraud or to deceive customers, even if the fraud itself isnt completed. 2. Regulatory Violations Even if prosecutors dont pursue criminal charges, such behavior can trigger : OCC enforcement actions ( unsafe, unsound, or deceptive banking practices ) ; FDIC Section 8 ( e ) removal and prohibition orders ( employees can be barred from the banking industry ) ; CFPB penalties for unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices ( UDAAP ).

Under FCRA 611 ( a ), the credit bureaus are obligated to conduct a reasonable reinvestigation into disputed items. Despite my detailed dispute, the credit bureaus responded with a generic statement claiming the account had been verified as accurate. However, no real verification ever occurred. A proper verification under federal law requires Wells Fargo to provide supporting documentation such as : A signed application bearing my signature The original contract for credit services Records of identity verification used at account opening Copies of monthly statements A complete payment history Transaction records Documentation showing how the $860.00 delinquency developed Any written correspondence allegedly mailed to me The internal account history logs Customer service notes Evidence showing the accounts opening date, usage, and closure Copies of any credit-limit agreements or disclosures Evidence of any collection activity None of these items were provided to me at any time. The credit bureaus failed to supply a Method of Verification as required under FCRA 611 ( a ) ( 6 ). This law states that when a consumer disputes an account and requests a MOV, the bureau must disclose the exact procedure used to verify the accountincluding what documents were reviewed, who verified the information, and how identity was confirmed. The bureaus have not produced any procedural details, documents, or evidence, which strongly suggests that no meaningful investigation was conducted. Instead, it appears the credit bureaus used the e-Oscar automated system, which simply forwards the dispute as a numerical code to the furnisher and receives a yes/no response. This system does not satisfy the legal standard of a reasonable reinvestigation when the account is alleged to be fraudulent or not belonging to the consumer. Furthermore, the reporting of the account shows several inconsistencies that reinforce that the account is not mine. The account history includes late payments and a charge-off date that do not match my financial history, my credit behavior, or any account I have ever owned. Because I never owned the account, Wells Fargo must be required to produce original documentation proving ownership. If they can not, FCRA requires that the account be deleted. Wells Fargo, as a furnisher of credit information, must comply with FCRA 623 ( a ) ( 1 ), which states : A furnisher shall not furnish information that it knows or has reasonable cause to believe is inaccurate. When I disputed the account, Wells Fargo was required under FCRA 623 ( b ) to conduct a full, complete, good-faith investigation. This investigation requires : Reviewing all relevant information Comparing account data with identity verification records Checking signatures and documents Determining whether fraud or a mixed file occurred Reviewing disputes thoroughly Correcting or deleting inaccurate information It does not simply require clicking a button to verify the disputed account. Additionally, Wells Fargo was required to mark the account as disputed by consumer under FCRA 623 ( a ) ( 3 ), yet this may not have been done properly or consistently. Failure to mark an account as disputed is misleading to lenders and violates federal law. Wells Fargo also has obligations under the federal reporting standards. If they fail to include accurate : date of first delinquency charge-off date balance history status codes compliance condition codes then the tradeline must be updated or removed. When I examined the reporting of the account, I found errors and incomplete data fields, further proving that the account is not mine and was not verified properly. Because this is an alleged Wells Fargo charge-off, several documents should exist if the account were real : Full transactional payment ledger Charge-off accounting schedules Internal servicing notes Collections activity log Communications register Copies of mailed notices Risk scoring and underwriting notes Application records stored in Wells Fargos system None of this has been presented in response to my disputes. Because none of these steps occurred, the account is clearly invalid. The harm caused by the false reporting continues to affect : my access to credit my credit score my financial opportunities my reputation as a responsible consumer All of these damages are occurring because Wells Fargo is reporting an account that does not belong to me and has not been verified in accordance with federal law. To summarize what happened : A Wells Fargo account is reporting on my credit file that I do NOT own. The reported past-due balance is $860.00. No payment history exists. No account opening documents exist. No evidence connecting me to this account exists. The account has harmed my credit score and financial standing. The reporting violates multiple FCRA provisions. The account is inaccurate and must be removed. Because I do not own the account, and because no proof of ownership has ever been provided, I am requesting CFPB assistance to ensure that the account is removed entirely from all credit reports.

narrative: , Date : Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) Subject : Formal Complaint Against Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., , , and for False and Misleading Credit Reporting, Failure to Verify Debt Ownership, and Failure to Provide Lawful Accounting and Note Documentation To Whom It May Concern, I. Summary of the Dispute Wells Fargo continues to report an alleged mortgage debt on my credit reports as though it is the creditor and lawful owner of the loan, even though Wells Fargo admitted in writing on , that it is merely the servicer and that the note holder is . Despite this admission, Wells Fargo has refused to : Produce or locate the original wet-ink promissory note, Identify who lawfully owns the note or whose credit or funds were used to originate the loan, Provide the double-entry accounting ledgers that would show the matching debit and credit entries for the alleged loan ( proving consideration was actually given ), and Identify where and to whom my last payment was distributed, despite claiming to act as servicer. inability or refusal to produce these required records under federal law demonstrates that the alleged debt is unverified, unsubstantiated, and is being falsely reported to consumer reporting agencies. II. Violations by Wells Fargo Bank , N.A . 1. Failure to Produce or Verify the Original Promissory Note Wells Fargo has not produced or located the original promissory note, despite stating they hold the note. Under Uniform Commercial Code 3-301, only a person entitled to enforce the instrument the legal holder of the original note may claim rights to collect or report a debt. Bank of New York v. Romero, 320 P.3d 1 ( N.M. 2014 ) The court ruled that mere possession or servicing of a note does not confer ownership or the right to enforce it ; a bank must show proper endorsement and chain of title. Kemp v. Countrywide Home Loans , Inc., 440 B.R. 624 ( Bankr. D.N.J. 2010 ) The court found that failure to produce the original note or proof of transfer undermines a creditors claim of ownership or right to enforce. Therefore, Wells Fargos reporting itself as creditor without producing the lawful note violates 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ) ( furnishing inaccurate information ). 2. Failure to Prove Funding and Consideration I have requested proof of whose credit or funds were used to finance the property at Under Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ), 15 U.S.C. 1601 et seq., creditors must disclose the source of loan funds and the identity of the true lender. Wells Fargo has not shown that it extended any lawful consideration or credit in exchange for my promissory note. This failure raises serious concerns about whether the debt was validly originated or whether Wells Fargo is misrepresenting its interest in the transaction. Carpenter v. Longan, 83 U.S. 271 ( 1872 ) The note and the mortgage are inseparable ; if Wells Fargo does not hold and fund the note, it can not claim rights to the mortgage or report the debt as its own. 3. Failure to Provide Accounting and Double-Entry Ledgers Under 12 U.S.C. 2605 ( e ) ( RESPA ), a servicer must respond to a Qualified Written Request ( QWR ) and provide accurate accounting information, including how payments were applied, to whom they were distributed, and the ledger entries reflecting the alleged loan. Wells Fargo has failed to provide : The double-entry accounting ledgers showing debits and credits for the alleged loan, The application and distribution of my last payment, and The complete payment history identifying all counterparties and transfers. This omission constitutes a violation of RESPA 2605 ( e ) and Regulation X ( 12 C.F.R. 1024.36 ), which require the servicer to provide requested servicing information within 30 business days. Case law : Rawlings v. Dovenmuehle Mortgage , Inc., 64 F. Supp. 2d 1156 ( M.D. Ala. 1999 ) A servicers failure to provide requested account information violated RESPA. Marais v. Chase Home Finance LLC, 736 F.3d 711 ( 6th Cir. 2013 ) Servicers must provide complete account information and may be liable for damages for failing to comply with a QWR. 4. False and Misleading Credit Reporting By continuing to report itself as creditor while withholding proof of ownership, Wells Fargo has furnished inaccurate and misleading information to the credit bureaus in violation of : 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ) Furnishing inaccurate information, 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( D ) Failing to modify or delete inaccurate information after notice of dispute. III. Violations by , , and 1. Failure to Conduct Reasonable Reinvestigation Each bureau has been provided proof that Wells Fargo is only a servicer, not a creditor, yet all three continue to publish the inaccurate tradeline. This violates 15 U.S.C. 1681i ( a ) ( 1 ) and 1681i ( a ) ( 5 ), which require deletion or correction of unverifiable or inaccurate data. Cushman v. TransUnion Corp., 115 F.3d 220 ( 3d Cir. 1997 ) A CRAs reinvestigation must be reasonable given the evidence provided by the consumer. Dennis v. BEH-1, LLC, 520 F.3d 1066 ( 9th Cir. 2008 ) Failure to delete unverifiable data after dispute constitutes a violation of the FCRA. 2. Failure to Ensure Maximum Possible Accuracy Under 15 U.S.C. 1681e ( b ), CRAs must follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy. Continuing to report Wells Fargo as creditor despite proof to the contrary fails this standard. IV. Combined Consumer Harm Wells Fargos failure to provide ownership documentation, accounting records, and lawful note evidence combined with the CRAs refusal to correct the tradeline has caused : Damage to my credit score and reputation, Denial of financial opportunities, Emotional distress, and Violation of my statutory rights under FCRA and RESPA. V. Requested CFPB Action I respectfully request that the CFPB : Investigate Wells Fargo Bank , N.A . for violations of the FCRA, RESPA, and TILA ; Investigate , , and for failure to reinvestigate under FCRA 1681i ( a ) ; Order Wells Fargo to produce the original note, chain of title, accounting ledgers, and payment application documentation ; Order deletion or correction of the inaccurate Wells Fargo tradeline ; Require disclosure of the true owner of the alleged debt ; and Impose penalties for willful and negligent violations of federal consumer law. Supporting Documents Attached : My Qualified Written Request ( QWR ) dated ; Wells Fargos response admitting they are only the servicer ; Credit reports showing Wells Fargo listed as creditor ; Prior correspondence with all three credit bureaus. Conclusion Wells Fargos inability to produce the note, prove funding, account for payments, or show lawful ownership demonstrates that it is not the creditor and has falsely reported itself as such. The credit bureaus refusal to correct the inaccuracy further compounds this violation. I respectfully request that the CFPB take immediate enforcement action to ensure compliance with FCRA ( 15 U.S.C. 1681 et seq. ), RESPA ( 12 U.S.C. 2605 ( e ) ), and TILA ( 15 U.S.C. 1601 et seq. ). Description of the Issue I have maintained my AmEx account in excellent standing, never missed a payment, and consistently kept my balance well below my limit. Despite this, AmEx has repeatedly demanded that I pay a specific amount to retain my current credit limit, threatening to reduce or revoke my limit if I do not comply. AmEx representatives also indicated that they have reviewed my credit profile from other credit cards and are seeking to review my personal bank statements. There is no clause in my Cardmember Agreement authorizing AmEx to demand a discretionary payment outside of my regular minimum due, nor to condition my credit limit on the disclosure of my private banking information. I believe these actions violate federal consumer protections and constitute an unfair and deceptive practice. ________________________________________ 2. Potential Violations and Legal Grounds 1. Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), 15 U.S.C. 1681b Limits the permissible purposes for which a creditor can access or review a consumers credit report. Reviewing my credit profile from unrelated credit cards without a permissible purpose or my consent may violate this provision. 2. FCRA, 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ) Requires furnishers of information to provide accurate and complete information to credit bureaus. Any adverse reporting related to this extra-payment demand would be inaccurate and misleading. 3. Consumer Financial Protection Act ( CFPA ), 12 U.S.C. 5531 Prohibits unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices. Threatening adverse credit action or demanding bank statements and extra payments without a contractual or legal basis constitutes an unfair practice. 4. Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ), 15 U.S.C. 1666b Requires timely and clear disclosure of any changes to credit terms. AmEx has made no such disclosures. 5. Virginia Consumer Protection Act ( Va. Code 59.1-200 ) Prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in consumer transactions. ________________________________________ 3. Requested Action I respectfully request that the CFPB : 1. Investigate AmExs practice of demanding discretionary payments and reviewing unrelated credit profiles and bank statements. 2. Determine whether AmExs conduct violates the FCRA, CFPA, TILA, or applicable state law. 3. Require AmEx to cease the practice of demanding extra payments to maintain credit limits for accounts in good standing. 4. Ensure that no adverse or misleading information is reported to credit bureaus as a result of this situation. 5. Require AmEx to provide a written explanation of its decision-making criteria and to confirm in writing that my account will not be penalized for declining to make noncontractual payments. ________________________________________ Legal Footing Summary Law Protection Application FCRA 1681b Restricts permissible purposes for accessing credit reports. Prevents AmEx from reviewing other card data without cause. FCRA 1681s-2 ( a ) Requires accurate furnishing to CRAs. Stops false reporting if you refuse extra payment. CFPA 5531 Bans unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts. Covers threats tied to unlawful payment demands. TILA 1666b Requires disclosure of credit-term changes. AmEx failed to notify or document any change. VA Code 59.1-200 Protects from deceptive business acts. Supports consumer remedies under state law. ________________________________________ Sincerely, : All Rights Reserved : All Rights Reserved

narrative: ENHANCED CFPB COMPLAINT Wells Fargo Bank , N.A . Subject : Pattern of employee misrepresentation, false assurances, and systemic failure to maintain commercially reasonable security procedures under UCC Article 4A and OCC Safety & Soundness standards. On , I received four Wells Fargo Advanced Access codes by text from short-code between and Concerned that these codes indicated an attempted unauthorized login, I immediately contacted Wells Fargo. After being transferred through initial representatives, I was referred to Employee ID , who took the call at approximately During the call, she repeatedly stated that the messages were bank mistakes and routine internal activity, and she assured me percent that no one was trying to access my account. She opened as the record of that conversation, documenting her representation that the texts were internal and harmless. Minutes later, I called Wells Fargo again to verify this explanation. ID answered and reviewed . He confirmed that it had actually been opened as a fraud investigation and that the previous employees statements were false and misleading. He recorded the correction in File , noting that the earlier employee had provided incorrect information. During this second call, I requested the most basic safeguard any modern financial institution should support : that all account changes or transactions occur only in branch and only after my identity is verified using my debit card PIN, not a drivers license alone. The employee documented my request and replied that Wells Fargo does not have the technology or alert capability to inform or restrict branch personnel accordingly. The verbatim note entered in File reads : Customer wants every transaction and every change in the account to be done in branch. Customer must be verified with his debit card otherwise, no transaction or changes should be made. Customer also wanted everyone to be alerted including branch bankers about this but I advised that we dont have that type of alert capability. This admission exposes a severe deficiency in Wells Fargos security architecture. The bank lacks even the most fundamental tools to communicate customer-specific security restrictions internally or to enforce in-branch identity verification using a debit card PIN. Such a limitation renders its authentication procedures not commercially reasonable under UCC 4A-202 ( b ). Under 4A-204 ( a ), when a banks inadequate security procedures allow fraud despite a customers ordinary care, the loss is the banks responsibility. Beyond the technical failure, this incident adds to a clear, documented pattern of employee misrepresentation and deceit that I have experienced across multiple Wells Fargo interactions. In earlier cases ( see CFPB Case [ insert ] and OCC Case [ insert ] ), other Wells Fargo employees also provided false assurances including a claim that I had approved a wire transfer at a time when my wire-notification system had been disabled. This recurring behavior shows that misrepresentation is not exceptional at Wells Fargo ; it appears to be systemic and routine, reflecting either deliberate internal minimization or training deficiencies that mislead consumers about real risks. Such conduct violates the expectation of honesty and due care that national banks owe to their customers under federal consumer-protection laws and OCC Safety and Soundness standards ( which require institutions to : Maintain adequate internal controls and authentication processes ; Communicate operational restrictions effectively throughout the organization ; and Safeguard customer assets from unauthorized access. Wells Fargos own admission that it doesnt have that type of alert capability demonstrates failures on all three counts. It also raises serious questions under the Consumer Financial Protection Act ( 12 U.S.C. 5531, 5536 ) prohibiting unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices ( UDAAP ). Representing fraudulent-access alerts as routine internal mistakes, and assuring customers of safety when an investigation is already open, is deceptive conduct that erodes consumer trust and conceals material risks. The combined effect is a security posture so weak that a criminal with only basic technical skills could bypass Wells Fargos safeguards. The banks system relies not on layered authentication but on hope the benevolence or inexperience of thieves which is far below the standard of care expected of a federally regulated financial institution in 2025. Note to CFPB and Responding Institution : This submission contains verifiable data including exact timestamps, employee identification numbers, internal file references, and verbatim internal notations that document the banks admissions and procedural weaknesses. I respectfully request that Wells Fargos response address each factual element listed herein directly and not rely on generalized or template language. A generic response will not resolve the core issues of misrepresentation and failure to maintain commercially reasonable security procedures under UCC 4A-202 and 4A-204 and the OCC Safety and Soundness Standards ( 12 C.F.R. 30 Appendix A ). Please ensure any Wells Fargo reply includes : A factual explanation of why four Advanced Access codes were generated on and what triggered them ; An internal confirmation or denial that File was opened as a fraud investigation ; A technical explanation of Wells Fargos current branch-notification and debit-card-PIN verification capabilities ; and Identification of which business unit or executive officer is accountable for these security controls.

narrative: This complaint concerns American Express and American Express Companys continuing failure to provide documentation constituting a complete credit application as required under 12 C.F.R. 1002.2 ( f ) and related record-retention and disclosure requirements. Despite repeated written requests beginning , and a prior CFPB complaint ( , filed ), American Express has not produced the executed credit agreement, any security or collateral documentation, or any record identifying the secured or transferee party responsible for the receivable associated with my credit-card account ending . In letters dated ( , ) and ( , ), the company : Instructed me to obtain the records through subpoena, implying such documents exist and are under the companys control ; and Simultaneously asserted that the account has not been sold, transferred, or securitized. These positions are materially inconsistent. Under 12 U.S.C. 24 ( Seventh ), national banks may lend, deal in, and pledge notes and receivables only under proper documentation and authority. Refusing to disclose or confirm such documentswhile maintaining active credit reporting and invoking rights under a contract they will not producecreates a compliance gap under Regulation B and TILA. American Expresss Cardmember Agreement ( page 4 ) explicitly states that the company may sell, transfer, or assign this Agreement and your Account. That contractual clause confirms that such transfers are contemplated and executed as part of Amexs banking operations, underscoring the need to identify the responsible officer or department that ensures compliance with the ECOA complete-application standard ( 12 C.F.R. 1002.2 ( f ) ). Disclosure and Certification Concerns In its Form for the quarter ended , American Express Companys CEO and certified under Exchange Act Rules 13a-15 ( e ) and 15d-15 ( e ) that disclosure controls were effective and all material information was properly evaluated. Despite being on notice of my CFPB complaint and the companys subpoena instruction, the filing contains no disclosure under Items 103 ( Legal Proceedings ) or 105 ( Risk Factors ) related to consumer-credit documentation or Regulation B compliance. This omission calls into question the adequacy of the companys internal compliance evaluation and executive-level certification process. I believe the absence of these issues from the misrepresents the state of Amexs consumer-credit documentation practices to both regulators and investors. Supporting Authorities Federal Law 12 U.S.C. 24 ( Seventh ) Governs a national banks lending and note-dealing powers, requiring lawful documentation of such transactions. 12 C.F.R. 1002.2 ( f ) and 1002.12 Require creditors to obtain and retain a complete credit application, including any information regularly considered such as collateral. 15 U.S.C. 1635, 1641 ( TILA ) Require creditors to disclose credit terms and assignment rights. 15 U.S.C. 1681b ( FCRA ) Limits credit reporting to instances supported by a valid and permissible purpose. Stat. 137.16 ( 2 ) Requires retention of any electronic credit agreement in a form capable of accurate reproduction. Wis. Stat. 409.203 ( 3 ) ( a ) A security interest attaches only when supported by an authenticated security agreement. Wis. Stat. 409.210 ( 2 ) Grants debtors the right to request the identity of the secured party and a description of collateral. SEC Rules Regulation S-K Item 601 ( b ) ( 10 ) Requires filing of material contracts such as receivables purchase or securitization agreements. Regulation S-K Items 103 & 105 Mandate disclosure of pending regulatory or legal issues and material operational risks. The closure and forfeiture occurred without any adverse-action notice explaining specific reasons, contrary to federal consumer-protection requirements. . Grounds for Complaint . Violation of the Fair Credit Billing Act ( ) and Regulation Under 15 U.S.C. 1666 and 12 C.F.R. 1026.13, a consumer has the right to dispute billing errors. Creditors are prohibited from retaliating against a consumer for exercising this right. Closing my account after validating my disputes constitutes retaliatory action and violates the intent and protections of the FCBA. . Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices ( UDAAP ) Consumer Financial Protection Act of ( 12 U.S.C. 5531 ) American Express engaged in conduct that meets the statutory definition of unfair and deceptive : Unfair : The closure caused financial harm, including loss of credit availability and confiscation of valuable reward points, which was not reasonably avoidable by me and served no legitimate benefit to consumers. Deceptive : Marketing of Membership Rewards as earned and redeemable value while reserving the ability to confiscate them without due process is materially misleading. Such conduct falls squarely within the CFPBs UDAAP enforcement jurisdiction. . Violation of the Equal Credit Opportunity Act ( ECOA ) and Regulation Under 15 U.S.C. 1691 ( d ) and 12 C.F.R. 1002.9, creditors must provide a written adverse-action notice specifying the reasons for closing a credit account. I received no formal adverse-action notice explaining the specific factors that led to the closure of my accounts. High dispute activity is neither a legitimate nor a lawful reason to deny or close credit when those disputes were resolved in the consumers favor. Failure to provide a compliant notice constitutes an additional Reg violation. . Deprivation of Earned Rewards Deceptive Practice American Expresss seizure of accrued Membership Rewards points without providing their cash or equivalent value breaches the principle of good faith and fair dealing implied in every consumer contract. Points have tangible redeemable value ( e.g., travel, statement credit, merchandise ). Over , I exchanged multiple emails with Wells Fargos Senior AVP Sales Support , , reiterating that I would not sign any loan relying on an appraisal that materially misrepresented my home and providing additional documentation and prior appraisal evidence. In one of those emails I explicitly stated : I will not sign any loan application that relies upon or incorporates an appraisal that materially misrepresents the nature and value of my home. On , Wells Fargo acknowledged the revised appraisal was unsupported and said it would escalate to a desk review at no cost to me ; however, Wells Fargo ultimately refused to correct the valuation and continued pressing me to proceed with the loan based on the flawed appraisal. Illusory Appeal Process Wells Fargos internal process gave the appearance of a fair and good-faith review but, in practice, provided only illusory assurances : At each stage Wells Fargo required additional forms, supporting documents, and iterations of my request, which I promptly provided. Despite the exacting evidence I submittedincluding prior appraisals, MLS listings, photographs, and a 360 virtual tourthe outcome did not change. Wells Fargo continued to insist that I proceed with a refinance based on an appraisal that clearly undervalued my home, to its advantage and to my detriment. I was incredulous that Wells Fargo would so vigorously defend an obviously flawed appraisal and perpetuate this treatment on an existing customer ; this leads me to question how other consumersespecially non-customersare treated in similar processes. This pattern left me with the reasonable but mistaken belief that Wells Fargo was treating my complaint in good faith when in fact the outcome was predetermined. Why the Error Is Material The $50000.00 figure for a full-bathroom difference comes from the original appraisers own stated adjustment schedulenot from any Wells Fargo methodology . This artificially increased my loan-to-value ratio, exposed me to a higher interest rate, and undermined my ability to proceed on fair terms. Lost opportunity : I ultimately abandoned the refinance with Wells Fargo and proceeded with another lender. Reasonable compensation for my time spent attempting to correct the error, which I will substantiate upon request. This complaint is directed at Wells Fargo the institution, not at any individual employee. While was my primary contact, the outcome reflects institutional handling and decision-making. Conclusion I complied with Wells Fargos procedures, promptly supplied evidence, and flagged a clear, material defect. sub_issue: Funds not handled or disbursed as instructed
narrative: Follow up to case : Bank set off account without proper action. Under the Uniform Commercial Code ( ), banks exercise a right of setoff by applying funds in a customers deposit account toward debts owed to the bank. However, this right is limited by law and must be exercised in compliance with good faith and commercially reasonable practices. Key Principles : Authorization Requirement : A setoff may only be exercised if clearly authorized by the account agreement. Ambiguous or undisclosed terms are not sufficient to allow unilateral withdrawal of funds. Duty of and : Even where a contractual setoff clause exists, the bank must act in good faith and in a commercially reasonable manner. Seizing funds without notice or while simultaneously failing to process agreed automatic payments does not meet this standard. of Obligations ( ) : A bank must honor properly payable items ( e.g., checks or authorized electronic transfers ) once they have been accepted for processing. Exercising setoff in a way that causes the dishonor of legitimate payments is inconsistent with the UCCs requirements. Application to : Lack of Informed Consent : I was never explicitly told that setoff would authorize Wells Fargo to withdraw funds from my account without my signature or contemporaneous authorization. Failure of : Wells Fargo failed to process my scheduled automatic payments ( an error on its part ), then used setoff to seize funds without notice, exacerbating financial harm. : setoff was applied before honoring my e-check to my attorney, resulting in a dishonored check. This contravenes , which restricts banks from prioritizing setoff over valid payment obligations. Lack of Notice : Reasonable notice is generally expected before setoff so that the customer can make alternative arrangements. Wells Fargo provided none. provides banks with a limited right of setoff, that right is constrained by principles of good faith, proper authorization, and fair dealing. actionsfailure to process auto-payments, unilateral of funds without warning, and dishonoring of other legitimate paymentsrepresent a misuse of setoff authority and a violation of these legal standards.

narrative: WFBNA Auto is furnishing an installment auto loan account as a derogatory Collection/Charge-off with a balance of $10000.00. The account appears across all three major credit bureaus as derogatory, with status comments such as : Charged off as bad debt Profit and loss write-off ( ). Unpaid balance reported as a loss by the credit grantor ( ). Charged off account Auto ( ). The reporting of this account is inaccurate, contradictory, and unlawful for multiple reasons : 1. Contradictory Balance and Charge-off Status A charge-off occurs when the creditor moves an unpaid debt into a loss category for accounting purposes. By definition, a charge-off reflects that the creditor has written off the debt as uncollectible. However, WFBNA continues to report a current balance of $10000.00 and a past due balance of $10000.00. It is not legally consistent to report both a charge-off and an active, past-due balance at the same time. This contradictory reporting violates 15 U.S.C. 1681e ( b ) of the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), which requires that furnishers ensure maximum possible accuracy. 2. Double Punishment Through Dual Statuses The account is being reported as : Collection Charge-off Derogatory Each of these is a derogatory designation, but reporting them all simultaneously creates the illusion of multiple negative events rather than one. This unfairly multiplies the impact on my credit file. This over-reporting constitutes false and misleading furnishing under 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ), which prohibits reporting information known or reasonably believed to be inaccurate. 3. Improper Reporting of Past Due Amounts A charged-off account should not continue reporting as Past Due $10000.00 because the account has already been classified as a charge-off and written off the books. Continuing to list the account as both charged-off and past due exaggerates the delinquency and paints me as more irresponsible than the facts support. This is deceptive, misleading, and unlawful under the FCRA. 4. Failure to Conduct Reasonable Reinvestigation I have disputed this account. Despite my dispute, WFBNA has continued to report the same derogatory information. Under 15 U.S.C. 1681i ( a ), the credit reporting agencies and furnishers are required to conduct a reasonable reinvestigation. A reasonable reinvestigation can not result in the same contradictory, inaccurate reporting that currently exists. This demonstrates that no actual investigation was performed, only a superficial verification with no documentary proof. 5. Extending the Damage Beyond the Original Default The account shows a Date Last Active of but is still being updated monthly as of . Each new update re-ages the derogatory account, keeping it active in my credit file and prolonging its negative impact. This is an abuse of the reporting system and violates the principle that negative information must be reported accurately and within fair time limits. 6. Material Harm to the Consumer Because of this reporting, my credit scores are artificially depressed. Creditors, lenders, landlords, and even potential employers reviewing my file see the false impression that I am : Currently delinquent. Still owing $10000.00. In charge-off status. In collections. This quadruple-negative portrayal is inaccurate and defamatory. As a direct result, I have suffered denials for credit applications, higher interest rates, reputational harm, and limited access to financial opportunities. 7. Willful and Negligent Noncompliance WFBNA has continued this reporting despite my disputes, making them liable for both willful noncompliance ( 15 U.S.C. 1681n ) and negligent noncompliance ( 15 U.S.C. 1681o ) with the FCRA. Their conduct shows a reckless disregard for the truth and for my consumer rights.
